title: Ignatius, again
tomorrow: words or silence: which way of praying does Carmel choose?

lines: NO ADVENTURE STORIES IN THE HOUSE.
cards: Scroll for an hour and it's fun while it lasts. Then you put the phone down, and something feels a little flat.

Hold that, because here's the odd detail. Íñigo de Loyola, a Basque soldier, is laid up after a cannonball wounds his leg. Bored, he asks for adventure stories, tales of knights. The house doesn't have any.
All anyone can bring him is a life of Christ and a book of saints. How does a man find God because the library was bad?

teach.h: THE KNIGHTLY DREAMS LEFT HIM DRY.
teach.b: He reads what's there, and he daydreams. Some daydreams are about a great lady and deeds of arms. Others are about doing what the saints did.

Then he notices something, as he tells it in his own story. The knightly daydreams delight him while they last, but afterward leave him dry and unhappy. The saintly ones leave him content even after they're over.
That's the puzzle solved: God reached him through the aftertaste. Not through the rush, but through what stayed.
Ignatius, as he came to be called, built a whole way of prayer from that noticing, the Spiritual Exercises, and his companions, the Jesuits, took the motto for the greater glory of God.
His big idea is the one on today's card: God in all things. Not only in church. In a meal, a walk, a hard conversation, a bad library.

teach.h: IN HIM WE LIVE, AND MOVE, AND ARE.
teach.b: Paul says it to the Athenians, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "in him we live, and move, and are."

Here's the one to tell a friend: Ignatius taught a short prayer called the examen, looking back over the day to notice where God was and where you turned away. One honest look at the hours that just happened.
If God is in all things, then the day you just had is full of clues.

how: Jesuits and many lay Catholics make the Spiritual Exercises of Ignatius, sometimes as a retreat, and pray the examen, a short look back over the day for where God was present.

o: a bishop who wrote down the Church's laws
a monk who never once left his monastery
a soldier who found God by noticing his days

games.q: the soldier in bed — tap the pairs.
p: a way of prayer built on noticing
look back over the day for God

s: Ignatius asked for a life of Christ while he recovered
he asked for tales of knights. the house only had a life of Christ and a book of saints.
Ignatius noticed how his daydreams left him afterward
the knightly ones left him dry; the saintly ones left him content.
God in all things means God is found mainly in church
in a meal, a walk, a conversation: in all things.

games.q: you're Íñigo, laid up for weeks, bored, with only a life of Christ and a book of saints. what do you do?
o: read, daydream, and notice how each daydream leaves you.
refuse the books and wait for adventure stories.
force yourself to stop daydreaming entirely.
games.why: he read and daydreamed, and noticed the aftertaste: the knightly dreams left him dry, the saintly ones content. that noticing became the Spiritual Exercises.

practice: Look at one ordinary object near you: a cup, a shoe, a window. Look at it long enough to notice something new about it: its color, a scratch, who made it.
If you pray, you can ask where God is in this one small thing; if not, simply let it be worth noticing.

wordCard.voice: Ignatius. The wounded soldier from Loyola who found God by noticing what his daydreams left behind.

orig.note: Latin: for the greater glory of God. the Jesuit motto.

carryVoice: Keep this: all things, even a bad library and an ordinary cup, can carry God. That's today.
